issues.item: Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
issues.explanation: For a police trauma profile, the trigger set is not clinically coherent as a group. Physical touch can fit, but crash imagery and burnt smell together suggest a road traffic accident or fire-related trauma rather than police-related trauma, and there is no supporting memory or appraisal content tying these cues back to police trauma.

issues.item: Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
issues.explanation: The contamination appraisal is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. It more commonly fits sexual assault or severe physical violation. Here it is unsupported by the trigger and memory items, which focus on fragmented recall and guilt rather than shame/violation themes.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Hypervigilance towards dangerous people could occur after police trauma, but in this profile it is weakly supported because the triggers point toward accident/fire cues rather than interpersonal threat cues. This creates a cross-node mismatch between maladaptive strategy content and the rest of the selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: 'Contamination/feeling dirty' is more typically coherent with sexual assault or severe bodily violation trauma. In a police-trauma profile, it is hard to reconcile this appraisal unless there are other items indicating sexualized assault, humiliating bodily violation, or related memory content, which are absent here.

A tactile trigger of general physical touch would usually imply trauma involving bodily contact/restraint. That could occur in police trauma, but in this profile there is no supporting memory or appraisal content about physical restraint, assault, or contact-based threat. Given the rest of the profile emphasizes authority/police cues, danger, mistrust, and guilt, this broad touch trigger stands out as insufficiently supported and clinically hard to place.

vignette:
Rohan had always considered himself a meticulous man. As a graphic designer, his world was one of grids, alignments, and careful planning. Now, at forty-one, that meticulousness had curdled into something else entirely. Before every client call, he would spend an hour mapping out conversational trees, scripting his responses to every conceivable question. The spontaneity he once enjoyed was gone, replaced by a rigid, exhausting vigilance. He was certain that one wrong word, one misstep, could lead to disaster. It was a belief that had taken root eight months ago, on the night his front door splintered inward.

He and his wife had been watching a movie when the explosion of sound and light tore their quiet evening apart. Men in heavy tactical gear swarmed his living room, their faces obscured by helmets, their commands a garbled roar. He was thrown to the floor, the rough texture of his own rug scraping his cheek. The air filled with an acrid, chemical smell, a burnt odour that clung to the back of his throat. He later learned it was from a flashbang grenade. He also learned that his neighbour, the man he'd shared beers with over the fence for five years, had called the police with a fabricated story about a drug operation. The raid was a mistake, a case of "bad information." An apology was offered, but the damage was absolute. He had been betrayed by someone he trusted, and the people in uniform who were meant to protect had instead become the source of his deepest terror.

In the weeks that followed, the world began to shrink. The smell of his wife's burnt toast sent him staggering back from the kitchen, heart hammering against his ribs. A police car idling at a traffic light was enough to make him miss his exit on the freeway, his hands slick with sweat on the steering wheel. Even the uniformed security guard who patrolled his office building became an object of intense scrutiny. Rohan would watch him from his desk, tracking his movements, his mind racing to assess the threat. He had come to believe that the world was a fundamentally dangerous place, and that danger could be wearing any uniform. People, he now knew, simply could not be trusted.

When his wife, Priya, tried to talk to him about that night, the words would catch in his throat. He could see it all in his mind's eye-the splintered wood of the door, the blinding light, the boot on his back-but he could not find a way to assemble the sentences. "I know what happened," he'd stammer, "but I can't... I lose the thread." The attempt would leave him exhausted and awash with a profound, suffocating guilt. He felt he should have done something different, been more prepared, somehow prevented the violation of his own home. The failure to explain it felt like a failure to have controlled it.

His careful planning, once a professional asset, was now a cage. Priya had stopped asking about booking holidays. Talk of the future-a vacation next year, a five-year plan-was met with a wall of anxious silence from Rohan. How could he plan for a future when he couldn't even guarantee his safety on the walk from the subway to his apartment? He scanned every face on the train, his body tense, always on the lookout for the person who might bring it all crashing down again. This constant state of alert had cost him a major client at work and was now fraying the edges of his marriage. It was Priya who finally gave him the ultimatum, her voice gentle but firm. She told him she couldn't live in a permanent state of waiting for the other shoe to drop. He is in therapy now not because he believes he can be fixed, but because he is terrified of losing the one person he still desperately wants to trust.
